title: Young and Old Stars Found in Andromeda's Halo
caption: Stars in the halo of the Andromeda Galaxy, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Andromeda Galaxy, Messier 31, NGC 224 · constellation Andromeda

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: This field of stars lies in the halo of the Andromeda Galaxy, also known as M31, the nearest spiral galaxy to our own. The halo is a spherical cloud of stars surrounding the galaxy, which is 2.5 million light-years from Earth.

The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. At the time it was described as the deepest visible-light image of the sky ever made, and it resolves roughly three hundred thousand individual stars.

Depth matters here because the picture records bright giant stars as well as faint dwarf stars. By looking at how the stars are spread across a range of colours and brightnesses, astronomers can estimate the age of the halo's population. That same method, reading the ages of stars from their colours and brightnesses, is one of the main tools astronomers use to date stellar populations.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the halo in visible and near-infrared light at 606 nm and 814 nm, with a synthetic green channel. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Individual stars in Andromeda's halo are far too faint to see by eye, and only very deep Hubble exposures can pick them out.
